title: Fast Walkers in Their 80s Have Sharper Minds
hook: A study of people 80 and older found the fastest walkers had about half the risk of cognitive decline — one more sign that a strong stride and a strong brain go together.
key_points: A study followed people 80 and older, comparing those with notably fast, steady gaits to their peers.
The fastest walkers had roughly a 50% lower risk of cognitive decline.
Gait speed is emerging as an easy, visible marker of brain health, not just leg strength.
The link runs both ways: walking speed reflects brain health, and staying active helps protect it.
content_html: Walking speed doesn't just say something about your legs — it may say something about your brain, too. A new study following people 80 and older found that the fastest, steadiest walkers had roughly half the risk of cognitive decline compared with their peers, NPR's Allison Aubrey reports.
extra_html: Researchers see gait speed as an easy, visible marker of underlying brain health — a stride that stays quick and steady into your 80s likely reflects a nervous system and cardiovascular system that are both aging well. The relationship also runs in the other direction: staying physically active is one of the better-established ways to help protect the brain as you age, so a slowing walk can be as much a cue to move more as it is a symptom to watch. Either way, it's a reminder that the line between "physical health" and "brain health" gets thinner the longer you look at it.

related.title: Staying Strong as You Age
related.hook: The decline we associate with old age is partly the result of doing less. Staying active — in four distinct ways — keeps you independent far longer.

related.title: Keeping Your Brain Healthy
related.hook: No pill prevents dementia, but the habits that protect your heart turn out to protect your brain too.

related.title: How Much Exercise You Actually Need
related.hook: The headline number is smaller than most people fear: about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week — roughly 20-some minutes a day — moves the needle on your health.

flashcards.prompt: What did the study find about fast walkers in their 80s?
flashcards.back_html: Those with the fastest, steadiest gaits had roughly 50% lower risk of cognitive decline than their slower-walking peers — linking physical stride to brain health.

flashcards.prompt: Why is gait speed useful as a health marker in older adults?

choices.text: It's an easy, visible sign that may reflect brain health, not just leg strength
It's the only thing that predicts cognitive decline
It replaces the need for any other brain-health habits

flashcards.explanation_html: Researchers see gait speed as one accessible marker among many — a visible clue that often tracks with what's happening in the brain, not a standalone fix.
